---
title: "Where Bobcats Are, and Why?"
subtitle: "Question 2 — Bobcat"
---

The bobcat (*Lynx rufus*) is a mid-sized wild cat, about twice the weight of a
large house cat, with a short "bobbed" tail, tufted ears, and a spotted coat. It
is the most common wild cat in North America and ranges across most of the
continent. Bobcats are adaptable: they live in forest, chaparral, farmland, and
the green edges of cities, and they hunt mostly rabbits and rodents. In the Bay
Area they move through parks, watershed land, and suburban open space, which is
why their records are plenty and their occupancy is the question to ask:
How much of the apparent pattern is bobcats and how much is people with cameras
and phones? The occupancy model is built to separate the two.

![A bobcat (*Lynx rufus*) in Bay Area open space. Photo: Don DeBold, [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Calero_Creek_Trail_Bobcat.jpg), [CC BY-SA 2.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/2.0). Illustrative only — not a study record.](media/images/lynx_rufus1.jpg){fig-alt="A bobcat standing in dry grass, side view" width="70%"}

## Occupancy

A raw map of bobcat sightings shows where people looked as much as where bobcats
are. An occupancy model separates those two. It treats each open-space unit as a
site visited repeatedly, models the chance of *detecting* a bobcat given that it
is present, and from that estimates the chance the unit is *occupied* at all. The
detection part absorbs the effort; the occupancy part is what's left.

The fit is a single-species occupancy model over 845 open-space units, built in a
fixed two-stage order: the detection sub-model first, then occupancy with the
detection structure held fixed. The covariate sets and the selection rule were
written down before any fitted number was looked at, so the result
is a test of a pre-registered model, not a search for one that fit.

## Detection is effort

The detection result is blunt. The single covariate is a per-visit record-count
effort proxy, and it dominates: more recording effort, far higher detection. 
Against a no-effort null the effort model is better by an AICc gap of 408.

This is the whole reason the occupancy model exists. A sightings map would read
that effort as bobcat distribution. The model reads it as effort and sets it
aside, so the occupancy surface underneath is not just a map of where people were
looking.

## What explains occupancy

With effort handled, three landscape parameters shape where bobcats are. The pattern
needs all three parts together — terrain, land cover, and human footprint. The
model that keeps only one of them falls far behind: a human-footprint-only or a
land-cover-only model is more than 40 AICc units below the full model, while the
full model and its near-twin carry 85% of the weight between them.

```{r}
#| label: fig-bobc-coef
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-cap: "Bobcat occupancy coefficients (logit scale, top model m_full), with 95% confidence intervals. Points right of the zero line raise the modelled chance a unit is occupied; points left lower it. Elevation is the strongest parameter (positive); human modification (gHM) is the clearest negative. Tree cover leans positive but its interval touches zero. Terrain aspect, slope, grass, and housing density do not separate from zero."
#| fig-alt: "A coefficient plot with nine occupancy terms on the vertical axis and effect size on the logit horizontal axis, a dashed line at zero. Mean elevation sits well to the right at about +1.4 with an interval clear of zero. Human modification sits to the left at about -0.56 with an interval clear of zero. Tree cover is positive at about +0.62 with an interval just touching zero. Grass, northerly and easterly aspect, slope, and housing density all sit near zero with intervals crossing it."

library(ggplot2)

# Occupancy (psi) coefficients from the top model m_full (Decision 31 fit).
# Estimates and SEs inlined from summary(mod); CI = estimate +/- 1.96*SE.
co <- data.frame(
  term = c("Mean elevation", "Slope", "Aspect (north)", "Aspect (east)",
           "Tree cover", "Grass cover", "Human modification (gHM)",
           "Housing density (log)"),
  est  = c( 1.4011, 0.0896, 0.1561, -0.0860, 0.6166, 0.4125, -0.5608, 0.1691),
  se   = c( 0.488,  0.275,  0.186,   0.168,  0.326,  0.272,   0.204,  0.168)
)
co$lo <- co$est - 1.96 * co$se
co$hi <- co$est + 1.96 * co$se

# Significance at the conventional 0.05 level drives colour, not the story —
# the caption states the directions in words.
co$sig <- ifelse(co$lo > 0 | co$hi < 0, "clear", "unresolved")

# Order by effect size for readability.
co$term <- factor(co$term, levels = co$term[order(co$est)])

col_pos <- "#2f6b3a"  # forest green — raises occupancy
col_neg <- "#9a4a2f"  # rust — lowers occupancy
col_nul <- "#8a8f9a"  # grey — interval crosses zero

co$col <- ifelse(co$sig == "unresolved", col_nul,
                 ifelse(co$est > 0, col_pos, col_neg))

ggplot(co, aes(x = est, y = term, color = col)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", color = "#b9b4a8") +
  geom_errorbarh(aes(xmin = lo, xmax = hi), height = 0.25, linewidth = 0.6) +
  geom_point(size = 2.6) +
  scale_color_identity() +
  labs(
    x = "Effect on occupancy (logit scale)",
    y = NULL
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),
    panel.grid.major.x = element_line(color = "#edeae3"),
    axis.text  = element_text(color = "#1a1a18"),
    axis.title = element_text(color = "#1a1a18"),
    plot.margin = margin(8, 14, 8, 8)
  )
```

**Elevation is the strongest parameter, and it is positive.** Bobcat occupancy rises
with mean unit elevation — the higher, less-developed units of the Coast Ranges
and Diablo are the strongholds. **Human modification is the clearest negative.**
As the gHM index rises, modelled occupancy falls: this is the coexistence limit
showing up directly in the numbers. **Tree cover leans positive** but its interval
just touches zero, so it reads as a lean, not a firm effect. Grass cover, slope,
terrain aspect, and housing density do not separate from zero in this fit.

Housing density enters positive but
unresolved, while gHM enters clearly negative. The two are correlated, and the
project lets gHM carry the human-pressure axis. Overall, the human parameters in bobcat occupancy are real and negative.

### The occupancy surface

The map below is the model-corrected result: predicted occupancy for each
open-space unit, after detection effort has been modelled out. It is the layer to
trust for distribution — not the raw sightings, and not the kernel density and hotspot that
follow.

```{r}
#| label: fig-bobc-psi
#| column: page
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-cap: "Predicted bobcat occupancy (ψ) by open-space unit, from the model-averaged occupancy fit. Darker green is higher predicted occupancy. Grey units are not modelled — they lack covariate coverage, so no prediction exists. The surface covers the 845 fitted units; the 284 grey units carry geometry only. Detection effort has been modelled out of this surface, which is what separates it from the raw record maps below."

library(sf)
library(leaflet)
library(dplyr)

# Rendered from site/, so data lives one level up at ../data/. A page-relative
# path is predictable here; here::here() can mis-anchor to site/ because Quarto
# plants its own project marker.
psi <- st_read("../data/processed/occu_bobc_pred_unit_3310.gpkg", quiet = TRUE) |>
  st_transform(4326)

# The psi layer carries no name field; the Gi* layer does, on the same unit_id
# key (join verified: every psi unit matches, no blank names). Bring the name in.
names_lookup <- st_read("../data/processed/hot_bobc_gistar_unit_3310.gpkg",
                        quiet = TRUE) |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  select(unit_id, unit_name)

psi <- psi |>
  left_join(names_lookup, by = "unit_id") |>
  mutate(unit_label = ifelse(is.na(unit_name) | unit_name == "",
                             paste0("Unit ", unit_id),
                             paste0(unit_name, " (unit ", unit_id, ")")))

modelled  <- psi[!is.na(psi$psi_pred), ]
notmodel  <- psi[ is.na(psi$psi_pred), ]

pal <- colorNumeric("Greens", domain = c(0, 1), na.color = "#cfccc4")

leaflet(options = leafletOptions(minZoom = 7)) |>
  addTiles(
    urlTemplate = "https://server.arcgisonline.com/ArcGIS/rest/services/Canvas/World_Light_Gray_Base/MapServer/tile/{z}/{y}/{x}",
    attribution = "Tiles &copy; Esri"
  ) |>
  addTiles(
    urlTemplate = "https://server.arcgisonline.com/ArcGIS/rest/services/Canvas/World_Light_Gray_Reference/MapServer/tile/{z}/{y}/{x}"
  ) |>
  # not-modelled units first, underneath, in flat grey
  addPolygons(
    data = notmodel,
    fillColor = "#cfccc4", fillOpacity = 0.55,
    color = "#9a978f", weight = 0.5, opacity = 0.8,
    label = ~paste0(unit_label, " — not modelled (no covariate coverage)")
  ) |>
  # modelled units on top, green scale
  addPolygons(
    data = modelled,
    fillColor = ~pal(psi_pred), fillOpacity = 0.8,
    color = "#4a4a48", weight = 0.4, opacity = 0.7,
    highlightOptions = highlightOptions(weight = 2, color = "#222", bringToFront = TRUE),
    label = ~sprintf("%s — \u03c8 = %.2f (SE %.2f)", unit_label, psi_pred, psi_se)
  ) |>
  addLegend(
    position = "bottomleft", pal = pal, values = c(0, 1),
    title = "Predicted occupancy (\u03c8)", opacity = 0.8
  ) |>
  addControl(
    "<div style='font-size:11px;line-height:1.3;max-width:200px'>
     Grey = not modelled (no covariate coverage), <b>not</b> low occupancy.
     Effort is modelled out of this surface.</div>",
    position = "topright"
  ) |>
  # fitBounds MUST be last, or the auto-fit overrides it
  fitBounds(-123.53354, 36.85065, -121.20830, 38.86399)
```

This surface is where the effort correction pays off. A raw sightings map would
put the darkest color wherever recording is densest — near trailheads, near
cities. The occupancy model moves the results to where the *landscape* supports
bobcats: up in elevation, away from human modification. Where the two disagree is
the effort bias made visible, and it is the heart of Question 5.

## Kernel Density and Hot Spots

The occupancy surface is the model-corrected view. Two descriptive layers sit
alongside it, and both carry the effort problem the occupancy model was built to
mitigate.

**Kernel density.** A smoothed surface of where bobcat records fall. The smoothing
scale — the bandwidth — is set by a pre-registered rule, because the default bandwidth collapses toward a tiny bandwidth
that just maps the densest clusters of *effort*. Even with the rule,
a kernel-density surface of opportunistic records maps detection effort as much as
bobcat density. It is shown as a descriptive layer, not as an abundance estimate.

```{r}
#| label: fig-bobc-kde
#| column: page
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-cap: "Kernel-density surface of bobcat records (500 m, precise records only). Darker green is higher record density. The colour follows a square-root stretch, not a linear one: density is heavily right-skewed, so a linear scale would show only a few peak cells and wash out the rest — the stretch makes the pattern visible but visually lifts the low values, so read colour as relative pattern, not absolute density. Masked and out-of-study cells are transparent, not zero."

library(terra)
library(leaflet)

k <- rast("../data/processed/kde_bobc_current_500m_3310.tif")

# Square-root stretch, capped near the 99th percentile of nonzero density so the
# handful of extreme cells do not blow out the ramp (values are right-skewed:
# max is ~400x the median). Masked cells stay NA -> transparent.
cap <- 0.00000398566624  # 99th percentile of nonzero density
ks  <- sqrt(clamp(k, lower = 0, upper = cap, values = TRUE))

# Tiger KDE green ramp; na.color transparent so masked area shows basemap.
ramp <- colorNumeric(
  palette = c("#F7FCF5", "#BAE4B3", "#74C476", "#31A354", "#006D2C"),
  domain  = c(0, sqrt(cap)),
  na.color = "transparent"
)

leaflet(options = leafletOptions(minZoom = 7)) |>
  addTiles(
    urlTemplate = "https://server.arcgisonline.com/ArcGIS/rest/services/Canvas/World_Light_Gray_Base/MapServer/tile/{z}/{y}/{x}",
    attribution = "Tiles &copy; Esri"
  ) |>
  addTiles(
    urlTemplate = "https://server.arcgisonline.com/ArcGIS/rest/services/Canvas/World_Light_Gray_Reference/MapServer/tile/{z}/{y}/{x}"
  ) |>
  addRasterImage(ks, colors = ramp, opacity = 0.75, project = TRUE) |>
  addControl(
    position = "bottomleft",
    html = htmltools::HTML(
      "<div style='background:#fff;padding:8px 10px;border-radius:4px;
                   box-shadow:0 1px 4px rgba(0,0,0,0.2);font-size:12px;
                   line-height:1.4;text-align:left;max-width:190px;'>
         <div style='font-weight:600;margin-bottom:5px;'>Record density</div>
         <div style='height:12px;border-radius:2px;margin-bottom:3px;
                     background:linear-gradient(to right,#F7FCF5,#BAE4B3,#74C476,#31A354,#006D2C);'></div>
         <div style='display:flex;justify-content:space-between;'>
           <span>low</span><span>high</span></div>
         <div style='margin-top:5px;color:#5a6070;font-size:11px;'>
           Square-root stretch. Reflects recording effort as much as density.</div>
       </div>"
    )
  ) |>
  # fitBounds MUST be last, or the auto-fit overrides it
  fitBounds(-123.53354, 36.85065, -121.20830, 38.86399)
```

**Hot spots.** A Getis-Ord Gi\* analysis flags units with significantly high or low
record counts relative to their neighbours. A raw-count hot spot is partly an observer-effort hot spot. So
each hot unit is cross-read against the effort surface and labelled — TRUSTED
where the cluster is not explained by effort, EFFORT-FLAGGED where it is. The map
shows the label, not just the count.

The result here is mostly an absence. After
false-discovery-rate correction, only **six units** are significant hot spots out
of more than eleven hundred, against **224** significant cold spots. Bobcat
records barely cluster into strong hotspots at all once the 
correction is applied. And of the six hot units, the effort cross-read trusts only
**four** — the other two coincide with recording-effort hotspots and are flagged
as suspect.

```{r}
#| label: fig-bobc-gistar
#| column: page
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false
#| fig-cap: "Getis-Ord Gi* hot- and cold-spot units for bobcat records, FDR-corrected. Red units are significant hotspots, purple units significant cold spots, faint grey not significant. Solid red is a TRUSTED hotspot; hollow red is a hotspot that coincides with a recording-effort hotspot and is flagged as effort-SUSPECT. Only six units are hot (four trusted, two suspect) against 224 cold — the weakness of the clustering is itself the result, and every count behind it reflects recording effort as much as bobcat presence. Source: sfdep Gi* with the Q5 effort cross-read."

library(sf)
library(leaflet)
library(dplyr)

hot <- st_read("../data/processed/hot_bobc_gistar_unit_3310.gpkg", quiet = TRUE) |>
  st_transform(4326)

# Tiger-site palette: hottest red, coldest purple, neutral grey.
col_hot <- "#B30000"
col_cold <- "#3F007D"
col_ns  <- "#CCCCCC"

ns_units   <- hot[hot$hotspot == "ns", ]
cold_units <- hot[hot$hotspot == "cold", ]
# Split the hot units by the Q5 effort verdict (Option B: fill treatment).
hot_trust  <- hot[hot$hotspot == "hot" & hot$q5_flag == "occ_hot_effort_not_TRUSTED", ]
hot_susp   <- hot[hot$hotspot == "hot" & hot$q5_flag == "occ_hot_effort_hot_SUSPECT", ]

lab_common <- function(d, verdict = NULL) {
  base <- sprintf("%s (unit %s)<br>Gi* z = %.2f, FDR p = %.3f",
                  d$unit_name, d$unit_id, d$gistar_z, d$gistar_p_fdr)
  if (!is.null(verdict)) base <- paste0(base, "<br><b>", verdict, "</b>")
  lapply(base, htmltools::HTML)
}

leaflet(options = leafletOptions(minZoom = 7)) |>
  addTiles(
    urlTemplate = "https://server.arcgisonline.com/ArcGIS/rest/services/Canvas/World_Light_Gray_Base/MapServer/tile/{z}/{y}/{x}",
    attribution = "Tiles &copy; Esri"
  ) |>
  addTiles(
    urlTemplate = "https://server.arcgisonline.com/ArcGIS/rest/services/Canvas/World_Light_Gray_Reference/MapServer/tile/{z}/{y}/{x}"
  ) |>
  # not significant — faint but visible context
  addPolygons(
    data = ns_units,
    fillColor = col_ns, fillOpacity = 0.18,
    color = "#b7b7b7", weight = 0.3, opacity = 0.4,
    label = ~lapply(sprintf("%s (unit %s) — not significant", unit_name, unit_id),
                    htmltools::HTML)
  ) |>
  # cold spots — purple
  addPolygons(
    data = cold_units,
    fillColor = col_cold, fillOpacity = 0.7,
    color = "#2a0057", weight = 0.4, opacity = 0.7,
    label = lab_common(cold_units)
  ) |>
  # trusted hot — solid red
  addPolygons(
    data = hot_trust,
    fillColor = col_hot, fillOpacity = 0.85,
    color = "#7a0000", weight = 1.0, opacity = 0.9,
    label = lab_common(hot_trust, "TRUSTED hotspot (not explained by effort)")
  ) |>
  # suspect hot — hollow red (effort-flagged)
  addPolygons(
    data = hot_susp,
    fillColor = col_hot, fillOpacity = 0.12,
    color = col_hot, weight = 1.6, opacity = 0.95, dashArray = "4 3",
    label = lab_common(hot_susp, "EFFORT-SUSPECT hotspot (coincides with an effort hotspot)")
  ) |>
  addControl(
    position = "bottomleft",
    html = htmltools::HTML(sprintf(
      "<div style='background:#fff;padding:8px 10px;border-radius:4px;
                   box-shadow:0 1px 4px rgba(0,0,0,0.2);font-size:12px;
                   line-height:1.5;text-align:left;'>
         <div style='font-weight:600;margin-bottom:5px;'>Gi* (FDR-corrected)</div>
         <div style='display:flex;align-items:center;gap:7px;'>
           <span style='width:15px;height:13px;background:%s;border:1px solid #7a0000;
                        display:inline-block;flex:none;'></span>Hotspot &mdash; trusted</div>
         <div style='display:flex;align-items:center;gap:7px;'>
           <span style='width:15px;height:13px;background:%s22;border:1.6px dashed %s;
                        display:inline-block;flex:none;'></span>Hotspot &mdash; effort-suspect</div>
         <div style='display:flex;align-items:center;gap:7px;'>
           <span style='width:15px;height:13px;background:%s;border:1px solid #2a0057;
                        display:inline-block;flex:none;'></span>Cold spot</div>
         <div style='display:flex;align-items:center;gap:7px;'>
           <span style='width:15px;height:13px;background:%s;border:1px solid #b7b7b7;
                        display:inline-block;flex:none;'></span>Not significant</div>
       </div>",
      col_hot, col_hot, col_hot, col_cold, col_ns
    ))
  ) |>
  # fitBounds MUST be last, or the auto-fit overrides it
  fitBounds(-123.53354, 36.85065, -121.20830, 38.86399)
```

## Summary

The bobcat occupancy
model *corrects* for effort and, where it does, its picture diverges from the raw
kernel density. The puma corridors in the next section do not depend on effort at
all — they are built from landscape resistance, not from sightings — so they
converge with the density surface for a different reason. Same region, two species,
two entirely different relationships between what was recorded and what is there.
